methods.name: Documented China income, bought and wired at a bank
methods.who: A foreign passport holder (境外个人) whose RMB is lawful current-account income earned in China, such as salary.
methods.cap: No yearly cap in the rule text. The amount is what your source documents and tax vouchers show.
methods.docs: Passport; source-of-funds material showing the amounts (for example employment contract and payslips); China tax vouchers.
steps: Collect the papers the rule names: passport, material showing where the RMB came from with the amounts, and the China tax vouchers for that income.
If tax on the income was never paid, settle it first. The tax office collects unpaid tax when an outward payment is reviewed.
Take the papers to your bank and ask to buy US dollars against lawful China income as a foreign individual. The bank checks that the documents are genuine and match the amount.
The bank converts at its selling rate. Compare the rate offered with the board before you accept.
Ask the bank to wire the dollars from your foreign-currency account to your own US account. A foreign individual remits from an FX account on ID.
For one payment above USD 50,000, ask the bank whether it wants a tax filing form as well as the tax vouchers.
Pay the commission and cable fee, keep the purchase and wire receipts, and keep the tax vouchers.
In the US, keep your FBAR and Form 8938 filings up to date for the China account, and report any income the money earned.
methods.pros: One wire, lowest sourced cost. No yearly cap in the text. The rule is written for exactly this case.
methods.cons: Works only for income you can document with tax vouchers. The bank may refuse if it doubts the documents.

methods.name: Proceeds of selling your China home
methods.who: A foreign individual who sold a home in China that they lawfully owned.
methods.cap: Not more than the sale price less the taxes of that sale, and not more than the amount on the tax certificate. Co-owners: your own share.
methods.docs: Passport; the registered transfer contract and proof of registration; the tax certificate for the sale; a notarised power of attorney if someone acts for you.
steps: Complete the sale and the transfer of title at the property registry. The bank will not remit before title has moved.
Pay the taxes of the sale and obtain the tax certificate. It caps what can be remitted.
Take passport, the registered transfer contract, proof of registration and the tax certificate to the bank.
The bank checks that the amount requested does not exceed the price less taxes and does not exceed the tax certificate.
Buy the dollars and wire them to your own US account. Keep the bank's annotated copy of the tax document.
In the US, report the sale on your return; China tax paid on the gain may be creditable.
methods.pros: Handled at the bank against documents. No yearly cap other than the net sale amount.
methods.cons: Tax on the sale must be paid first. An older rule still speaks of SAFE approval, so confirm the procedure with the bank.

methods.name: Emigrant asset transfer (former Chinese national)
methods.who: Someone who moved from mainland China and gained foreign citizenship or permanent residence, for lawful assets owned in China before that.
methods.cap: The amount SAFE approves. The bank may remit it once or in several payments.
methods.docs: Written application and the Personal Property Transfer form; foreign ID such as passport; proof of settlement abroad from a Chinese embassy or consulate, or with apostille; certificate that your household registration was cancelled; proof of income source and title; tax certificate.
steps: Confirm the assets were yours before you gained foreign status and are not frozen by a court or supervisory body.
Turn the assets into RMB and keep the sale and bank records that show where the money came from.
Obtain the tax certificate from the tax office where the income arose or the asset sits.
Get the settlement-abroad proof and the household-registration cancellation certificate.
File the application with the SAFE branch of your former household registration. Filing is in person and free.
SAFE decides within 20 working days and may extend once by 10. It issues a single-use approval valid nationwide.
Take the approval to a bank, buy dollars and wire them, once or in parts, within the approved amount.
In the US, keep FBAR and Form 8938 current and report any income or gain realised when the assets were sold.
methods.pros: The official route for capital that is not current income. No fee for the approval. One approval can cover the whole amount.
methods.cons: Paper-heavy. Needs hukou cancellation and consular or apostille proof. Applications above CNY 1 million from public officials or their close relatives may be checked with the supervisory authority.

methods.name: Inherited China estate
methods.who: A foreign citizen who lawfully inherited assets in China.
methods.cap: The amount SAFE approves. The bank may remit it once or in several payments.
methods.docs: Written application and the Personal Property Transfer form; foreign passport and ID; proof of settlement abroad; proof of inheritance such as a notarised inheritance certificate or will; the deceased's title documents; tax certificate.
steps: Obtain proof of your right to inherit, such as an inheritance or will notarisation.
Collect the deceased's title documents and turn the assets into RMB.
Obtain the tax certificate unless the rules say none is needed.
File with the SAFE branch of the deceased's last household registration. Estates from several people can be filed together at one of those branches.
SAFE decides within 20 working days, extendable once by 10, and issues a single-use approval.
Take the approval to a bank, buy dollars and wire them within the approved amount.
In the US, a bequest from a foreign estate above USD 100,000 in a year is reported on Form 3520.
methods.pros: An official route with no fee for the approval.
methods.cons: Paper-heavy and slow. The official guide's own wording is inconsistent, so ask the branch which conditions it applies.

methods.name: USD 50,000 yearly quota, on ID alone
methods.who: Only a 境内个人 (Chinese citizen with PRC ID) or a foreigner holding a Chinese Foreign Permanent Resident ID Card. A plain US passport holder does not have this purchase quota.
methods.cap: USD 50,000 of purchases per person per calendar year. Above it, documents of a genuine current-account use are needed.
methods.docs: Your own valid ID; the purchase application form filled in truthfully.
steps: Check that you hold a PRC ID or a Chinese Foreign Permanent Resident ID Card. A passport alone does not give the purchase quota.
Buy up to USD 50,000 in the calendar year at the counter or in the bank's app, stating the true purpose on the purchase form.
Wire the dollars for that purpose. Up to USD 50,000 a day leaves an FX account on ID; more needs documents with the amounts.
Repeat in the next calendar year if needed. Never use another person's quota or lend yours.
methods.pros: No documents within the quota. Can be done online.
methods.cons: Not open to an ordinary US passport holder. Slow for large sums: one quota per year. Each wire pays its own fees. The stated purpose must be a genuine current-account use.

methods.name: Change back unused RMB that came from your own foreign currency
methods.who: A foreign individual who earlier exchanged foreign currency into RMB and did not use it all.
methods.cap: The unused part of the original exchange, within 24 months of it. Without the original memo: USD 500 a day, or USD 1,000 on the day of departure past border control.
methods.docs: Passport and the original exchange memo.
steps: Find the original exchange memo. It is valid for changing back for 24 months from the exchange date.
Take passport and memo to the bank and change the unused RMB back.
Remit the foreign currency from your FX account on ID, or carry it within the cash limits.
methods.pros: Simple, on a memo you already hold.
methods.cons: Covers only money that entered as foreign currency within the last 24 months.

methods.name: Refund of a home purchase that fell through
methods.who: A foreign individual whose purchase money came from abroad and whose purchase was not completed.
methods.cap: The purchase money returned, plus reasonable interest earned while it was held.
methods.docs: Passport; the original payment and exchange vouchers; proof that the purchase failed; a written statement if you withdrew.
steps: Collect the original payment and exchange vouchers and the proof that the purchase failed.
The bank changes the RMB back and returns it the way it came: to the sending account abroad or your original FX account.
Keep the vouchers for your US records.
methods.pros: Returns by the original path, with interest allowed.
methods.cons: A narrow case. The money must go back where it came from.

methods.name: Wise, sending from CNY
methods.who: Not a mainland Chinese national; you work or have worked in China; you hold a China tax record from the last 3 years.
methods.cap: CNY 300,000 per transfer from a China bank app (CNY 50,000 from Alipay). Overall limit: your China salary after tax.
methods.docs: China tax records; identity verification on first use (1–2 working days).
steps: Check you qualify: not a mainland Chinese national, China work history, a tax record from the last 3 years.
Open a transfer to an account in your own name. Transfers to other people are not allowed.
Upload the tax record when asked. Your limit is set from salary after tax and does not expire.
Pay from your China bank app, at most CNY 300,000 per transfer, and read the fee and rate on the confirmation screen before you pay.
methods.pros: Done from a phone. Runs through a payment provider licensed in China.
methods.cons: Salary only, capped at what the tax records show. The fee and rate are not published in the guide. Large sums need many transfers.

methods.name: Cash from ATMs abroad with your China card
methods.who: A holder of a bank card issued in China.
methods.cap: CNY 100,000 equivalent per person per calendar year across all cards; CNY 10,000 per card per day.
steps: Use your own card only. Lending or borrowing cards to get around the cap is forbidden.
Stay inside CNY 10,000 per card per day and CNY 100,000 per person per year. Going over suspends overseas withdrawals for that year and the next.
Check your card's fee table before you travel; fees are not published in the rule.
methods.pros: No paperwork. Useful for small amounts.
methods.cons: Tiny yearly cap. Fees and rate unknown here. You end up with cash, and more than USD 10,000 crossing the US border must be reported.

methods.name: Carry US dollar banknotes out yourself
methods.who: Anyone who has lawfully bought the dollars first (by M01 or M05) and travels in person.
methods.cap: Up to USD 5,000 without a permit; above USD 5,000 up to USD 10,000 with a permit issued by the bank; more only in special cases with a SAFE permit. Cash withdrawal: USD 10,000 a day on ID.
methods.docs: Passport; the bank's carrying permit for USD 5,000–10,000.
steps: Buy the dollars lawfully first. Carrying cash is only a way to move dollars you were entitled to buy.
Withdraw banknotes, at most USD 10,000 a day on ID.
For more than USD 5,000 and up to USD 10,000, ask the bank for the carrying permit before you travel.
On arrival in the US, report on FinCEN Form 105 if you, or your family or group together, carry more than USD 10,000.
methods.cons: At most USD 10,000 a trip in ordinary cases. Travel cost and the risk of loss are not counted. Still needs a lawful purchase first.

methods.name: Leave it in RMB and spend it in China
methods.who: Anyone who expects to have costs in China.
steps: Use the balance for costs in China instead of converting it.
Keep filing the FBAR while your foreign accounts exceed USD 10,000 in aggregate at any time in the year, and Form 8938 above its thresholds.
Report interest the account earns on your US return, translated into dollars.
methods.pros: No conversion cost and no purchase paperwork.
methods.cons: The money is still in China and still in RMB. US reporting continues.

methods.name: Pay with the China card when you are abroad
methods.who: A holder of a bank card issued in China.
methods.cap: Spending is not counted against the USD 50,000 purchase quota. Other limits are set by the card.
steps: Pay genuine travel and living costs abroad with the card.
Check the card's foreign-transaction fee and rate first; they are not published in the rule.
methods.pros: No purchase paperwork. Uses the money without a wire.
methods.cons: It spends the money rather than moving it to a US account. Fees and rate unknown here.

methods.name: Send RMB abroad and convert it outside China
Splitting amounts, or borrowing or lending yearly quotas
methods.penalty: Watch list for the year of listing and the two following years; during that time every purchase or settlement needs documents with the amounts. Violations are punished under the Regulations.

methods.name: Underground banks, private money changers, offsetting swaps
methods.penalty: Warning, confiscation of illegal gains, fine up to 30% of the amount; serious cases 30% up to the full amount; criminal liability where a crime is made out (Art. 45).

methods.name: False or invalid documents to buy foreign currency
methods.penalty: The currency must be changed back; fine up to 30% of the amount; serious cases 30% up to the full amount; criminal liability where a crime is made out (Art. 40). Untrue documents: up to CNY 50,000 for an individual (Art. 48).

methods.name: Converting through virtual currency
methods.penalty: Exchange between legal tender and virtual currency in China is an illegal financial activity; institutions may not provide accounts or transfers; offenders are punished and may face criminal liability; losses are your own.

methods.name: Carrying cash above the limits without declaring it
methods.penalty: China: warning and a fine of up to 20% of the amount (Art. 42). United States: unreported currency above USD 10,000 can be seized, with civil or criminal penalties.

methods.name: Sham trade or other deception to move capital out
methods.penalty: Order to bring the money back; fine up to 30% of the amount; serious cases 30% up to the full amount; criminal liability where a crime is made out (Art. 39).
